topic: Lionfish Have No Predators in the Atlantic. Why Is Florida Asking People to Eat Them?
research_summary: The explainer rests on a well-documented chain: Indo-Pacific lionfish (Pterois volitans/miles) entered the western Atlantic via the aquarium trade in the mid-1980s to early 1990s, spread across the U.S. Southeast, Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico, and—lacking effective native predators and reproducing year-round—caused measured declines in native reef fish (a single lionfish reduced recruitment ~79% in a controlled experiment; a field study found a 65% decline in prey biomass in two years). Because eradication is considered impossible, NOAA launched an 'Eat Lionfish' campaign and Florida's FWC runs the Lionfish Challenge removal tournament (2025 marked its 10th anniversary with 30,000+ removed; the 2026 edition set a record of 36,187). Complications include ciguatera-toxin findings that led the FDA to withhold endorsement, and economic studies showing a thin commercial market. Comparable 'if you can't beat them, eat them' cases include Illinois rebranding Asian carp as 'copi,' and the Burmese python invasion in the Everglades (managed by removal rather than consumption) which caused severe native mammal declines. Operator source-pack URLs are used verbatim where claims rest on them; peer-reviewed and government open-access pages are preferred for checkability. Several abstracts behind paywalls (ScienceDirect) were avoided as source_url for quotes.
